doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing behind black artists in the segregated South
summary: His all-white band backed black artists, travelled the Green Book South, and was arrested in Norfolk for inciting a riot.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So what kind of things did you witness playing behind these black artists?

Well, the movie the “Green Book” every black artist I knew had the Green Book to know where they could stay, where they could eat. I played with many black artists that we couldn’t eat together and we certainly couldn’t stay in the same place together. I went with them sometimes and stayed in some of those horrible places they had to stay in. They were bad, bad. But that’s just, and it was those towns like they talk about in the “Green Book” you know, sundown towns. They couldn’t be out after dark or you had to have a damn good reason if the police stopped you, and they usually did, and if they said we just played a date here. And we had a bus, our band had an old Flexible bus that we had bunks in it and sofas and all that kind of thing back in the day, in the 60s. So they could travel with us. But I don’t know how many times we were stopped and they’d get on and they’d see black guys with white kids and it was like hell to pay. I got arrested once in Norfolk, Virginia. We were backing a group from Norfolk called the Showmen, a black quartet or quintet. And it was all white kids dancing. And they raided the place and we got arrested. Not the artists we were backing, we got arrested and our charge was inciting a riot. And it was kids dancing. There was no riot. My father was a First Sergeant

in World War II, boy he drove from Richmond down to Norfolk and he read them the riot act, to get us out of jail. We were arrested more than once. I was, myself. Because I played out with some other groups. But it was bad. Everything you’ve read about, then double that. It was sometimes scary. But we got through, we’re still living. I’ll tell you this, we had a pistol on the bus, I did. I know, I don’t know if the other band members did but I always had a pistol in my bag. It was some tough things. I — thank God, didn’t use it. But everything you saw in the “Green Book” triple that. Yeah. And everything you’ve read about it, triple that.
